program.name: MATS
program.roundStatusEvidence: Winter 2027 applications are closed. ... Stage 1: General application (closed September 6th)
program.nextRoundNote: No date announced for the next round; MATS offers a sign-up for future rounds. Late Winter 2027 applications go by email to applications@matsprogram.org.
program.programDates: Jan 19 – Apr 10, 2027 (12 weeks); optional 6–12 month extension
program.locationNotes: FAQ: main program is in person in Berkeley and London; historically most fellows are in Berkeley. Remote participation decided case-by-case, mostly by mentor preference ('Remote or part-time participation is a possibility depending on your circumstances and mentor'). J1 visas provided for US participation; no visa support for the London option. Extension can be from Berkeley, London, (Washington D.C. hub mentioned) or remote with mentor endorsement.
program.compensation: $19,200 stipend ($1,600/week for 12 weeks) plus $24k compute; housing, travel, office space, weekday lunch and dinner provided
program.commitment: Full-time, 40 hrs/week for 12 weeks (20 hrs/week possible case-by-case; not for J1 US participants)
eligibilityNotes: Must be 18 or older before the program start date (Jan 19, 2027).
Both US and non-US citizens are eligible; MATS provides J1 visas for US participation.
Prior AI safety experience is not required; all backgrounds and levels of experience welcome.
Candidates requiring a J1 visa cannot participate part time in the US (only remotely or from the UK).
Visa support is not available for the London option.

publishedTimeEstimate.text: “Plan to set aside a few hours for the initial application — more if you're applying to several tracks.” Includes a 20-minute reasoning test.

aiPolicy.summary: LLMs may not write any part of the application; the application's own policy permits only light grammar/spelling fixes on self-written text, concept lookups, brainstorming, and LLM critique of your draft, and bans LLM rewriting or generating from notes; answers are screened with AI detectors.
aiPolicy.quote: LLMs may not be used to write any part of your application unless specific work tests or forms explicitly permit it. MATS monitors for LLM use, and applicants found to have used LLMs may be disqualified.

stages.name: Stage 1: General application
stages.description: Account creation (first/last/preferred name, email) then the general application: AI-use policy acknowledgement, basic profile, optional publication record and prior engagement, two short-response questions (150–400 and 300–600 word targets), track selection with track-specific questions/writing samples, two referee contacts, a 20-minute reasoning test (Sparkwave), logistics, optional demographics, and network/consent. Open Aug 18 – Sep 6, 2026 (AoE).

stages.name: Stage 2, phase 1: Empirical assessments
stages.description: Empirical track only (and Biosecurity streams needing empirical ML skills): one or two standardized assessments of research taste and technical implementation; coding assessment takes 3–5 hours. Possibly reference requests. Content not published.

stages.name: Stage 2: Stream selection
stages.description: Advancing applicants apply to and rank streams within their tracks and answer stream-specific questions (usually short responses; some streams ask for a longer research proposal). References may be contacted for select candidates. Prompts not published.

stages.name: Stage 3: Mentor review
stages.description: October to early November: mentors review and rank applicants, often inviting interviews and work tests (vary by stream). Final matching uses mentor and applicant rankings.

stages.name: Offers
stages.description: Final offers sent early to mid-November 2026.

questions.helpText: You may list up to 5 publications below. If you have additional relevant publications, list them in the free text field at the end. Note: only one publication section is listed below initially. Additional sections will open as you complete all the required fields in previous sections. Publications are not required. Plenty of successful AI safety & security researchers start without a lot of (or any) past research experience. In general, try to list publications that highlight your skills & knowledge (e.g., research skills, technical skills, and domain expertise) relevant to any of MATS's research areas, even if they're not directly relevant to your current research interests or to the streams that you're most interested in. You may include other publications, but we will weigh sole/first/primary-author work more heavily. questions.prompt: Explain the framework you used to arrive at your top three ranked outcomes. Please address all three of the following:
questions.helpText: What's your north star? What single question or concern is most load-bearing in how you think about AI's effects on humanity? What criteria did you apply? When deciding which outcomes are most beneficial, what tests or filters did you actually run on each option? Be specific. Walk through your top three using the lens of those criteria. For each, briefly say why this option scored highly given the framework you laid out.

statedLength.text: Word target: 150–400 across all three parts. Minimum 150 words.

questions.notes: Short Response Question #1, part 2 (one of the two long-form answers). Followed by 'Reminder: follow the AI-use policy.' 'Word target' 150–400 with a hard minimum of 150.

questions.prompt: Tell us about a project, problem, or research question you've spent more than 20 hours on in the past 12 months.
questions.helpText: Pick something as relevant as possible to the track(s) you're applying to. Order of preference if you have multiple options: 1. AI safety, AI security, or biosecurity work directly; 2. AI, ML, or security work not directly safety-focused; 3. Other technical or analytical work. We'd rather see deep engagement on item 3 than shallow engagement on item 1. Don't pick something just because it's track-relevant if you didn't actually go deep on it. Please address each of the following separately in your response: What were you trying to figure out, and why did it matter? What did you actually do? Be concrete: methods, hours, and outputs (e.g paper, code, internal doc, decision, etc.). What surprised you? What did you do wrong, or what turned out to be suboptimal in retrospect? What's still unresolved or unknown?

statedLength.text: Word target: 300–600 across all five sub-questions. Minimum 300 words. Refer to specific resources (links, titles) where applicable.

questions.notes: Short Response Question #2 (second long-form answer). Followed by 'Reminder: follow the AI-use policy.'

questions.prompt: Writing sample #1
questions.helpText: Since you selected Policy & Governance or Strategy & Forecasting, you must upload at least one writing sample. We strongly recommend providing two writing samples. Leaving this blank is not disqualifying, but we will have a higher bar for advancement. We're looking for writing that demonstrates analytical reasoning about AI policy, AI governance, AI strategy, forecasting/futurism, or related topics. Examples we'd find informative: memos, briefs, policy reports, forecasts, scenario analyses, strategic analyses, blog posts, or academic papers. AI-related topics are preferred but not required. Non-AI writing that demonstrates similar reasoning skills is welcome. Don't write anything new for this application. Re-use writing samples from your publication record (just upload them here as PDFs), or upload writing samples you didn't include there.
questions.notes: Shown only if Policy & Governance or Strategy & Forecasting is selected. Marked [Required], though the help text says leaving it blank is not disqualifying (higher bar for advancement). PDF upload.

questions.prompt: Make a claim about advanced AI over the next 5 years that thoughtful, knowledgeable people would disagree about (i.e., don't state obvious claims). The claim should be strategically meaningful. Possible axes include (not an exhaustive list): capability arrival timelines, deployment dynamics, lab/government/military behavior, geopolitical balance, governance and regulatory trajectory, economic effects, dynamics inside a takeoff scenario.
questions.helpText: 1. State the claim precisely enough to be checkable 5 years from now. One or two sentences. 2. What probability do you assign to it? Why? Use whatever resolution feels honest (e.g., 37%, not "around 40%"). 3. What are some sub-questions or mechanisms that your estimate depends on? 4. Name a specific observation in the next 12 months that would update you ≥20 percentage points up, and a separate observation that would update you ≥20 points down. Be concrete — name the kind of result, announcement, paper, dataset, or event, not generic things like "more research happens". We want to see your strategic reasoning related to frontier AI, not just a "correct" answer.

statedLength.text: Word target: 200–500 across all four parts. Minimum 200 words.

questions.helpText: Also let us know if they participated in MATS (e.g., alum, mentor, staff). You are welcome to only share their affiliation if you don't want to share their name.
questions.notes: Conditional: required if 'Personal recommendation' is selected.
questions.condition: Only if you choose “Personal recommendation”

questions.prompt: Do you consent to us sharing your information with the broader MATS network for other opportunities (e.g., partner organizations, hiring orgs in the AI safety ecosystem)?
Standardized assessment of research taste (Empirical track, Stage 2 phase 1; exact content not published)
questions.notes: Apply page: 'Empirical assessments: You’ll complete one or two standardized assessments evaluating research taste and technical implementation skills.' Only for applicants who advance past Stage 1 in the Empirical track. Duration not published separately.

questions.prompt: Technical implementation / coding assessment (Empirical track, Stage 2 phase 1; exact content not published)
questions.notes: Apply page FAQ: 'If you advance to the empirical work test, the coding assessment takes 3–5 hours.' Biosecurity track page: streams requiring empirical ML skills include 'a standardized ML skills test' in Stage 2.

questions.prompt: Apply to and rank the specific research streams you'd like to join (Stage 2 stream selection)
questions.notes: Apply page: 'Stream selection: If you advance, you’ll apply to and rank the specific research streams you’d like to join.' FAQ: no cap on number of streams within tracks you progressed in. Exact form not visible.

questions.prompt: Stream-specific questions for each stream applied to (exact prompts not published; set per stream)
questions.notes: Apply page: 'When applying to streams, you’ll answer stream-specific questions. These are usually short responses, though some streams may ask for a longer research proposal.' Some Policy/Strategy stream pages say applicants will be asked to sharpen a mentor's project proposal or propose their own. Lengths vary by stream and are not published.

questions.prompt: Research proposal (some streams only; exact prompt not published)
questions.notes: Apply page: 'some streams may ask for a longer research proposal.' Winter 2027 stream page example (Policy/Governance & Strategy): 'During the application process, we will ask potential mentees to either a) sharpen these proposals into a more specific question incorporating their own interests, or b) propose their own projects.'

questions.prompt: Mentor interviews and work tests (Stage 3; vary by stream, not published)
questions.notes: Apply page: 'Mentors often invite applicants to complete interviews and work tests during this stage.' FAQ: 'Stage 3 interviews and work tests from mentors vary by stream.'
